To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Office for Human Research Protections (OHRP) are the primary federal agencies with jurisdiction over clinical registries.
clinical registries have evolved from retrospective to prospective and from observational to interventional, and that the federal regulations governing human subjects research apply to these systems.

clinical registries have evolved as an important tool for advancing the science and practice of medicine, and that the federal regulations governing clinical registries are complex, and must be understood by those designing and implementing these systems.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the application of the federal Common Rule to prospective clinical data collection activities that are not considered research, but which are nonetheless subject to the regulatory requirements of the federal government.
the development of a comprehensive, prospective clinical registry that can be used as a platform to advance the science and practice of neurosurgery.
the application of federal human subjects regulations to prospective patient care registres and the impact of this application to the design, implementation, and conduct of these systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the federal regulations that govern human subjects research apply to all prospective, longitudinal clinical registries.

clinical registries are subject to the regulations of the Food and Drug Administration, the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, the Common Rule, and other relevant federal laws.
the federal regulations that apply most directly to prospective patient care registres are those related to the protection of human subjects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
clinical registries, particularly prospective patient care registies, should be considered to have elements of research.

the National Neurosurgical Quality and Outcomes Registry (N2QOD) has been designed to meet all applicable federal requirements for the protection of human subjects, and to provide the highest quality data for the benefit of neurosurgical patients and providers.
the current federal regulations are not designed to address the unique needs of prospective patient care registires and, therefore, are not well-suited for the efficient design of such registries.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the design of a prospective, patient care registry should include a thoughtful and deliberate consideration of the federal regulations that apply, and that the process of obtaining institutional review board (IRB) oversight for these systems can be streamlined and simplified by following the recommendations provided in this article.

the design and implementation process of clinical registries can benefit greatly from the early involvement of institutional research review boards, as these entities can serve as important resources for the identification of appropriate research protections and the development of effective data acquisition and management strategies.
clinical registries are not exempt from the requirements of federal human subjects protection regulations.
